newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Analysts mixed on Israel market reform proposal.
newsitem.headline: Analysts mixed on Israel market reform proposal.

text.p: Israeli analysts were mixed in their reaction to capital market reform proposed by a government-appointed committee and said several measures are unlikely to be passed.

Zvi Hoffman of Meitav Investments said in general it was a positive document. "The best thing is the benefits that will be given to people who are saving for pensions. On the other hand it is difficult to see how they will tax unlinked bonds. Technically it is very difficult to do."
"The committee could not come out with a more revolutionary report and the entry of more institutional investors into the market will improve the market situation," he said.
He said the proposal to tax short-term savings will not pass. "Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu promised he would not do anything to harm savers."

Doron Tsur, head of research at Sahar Securities, said the direction is positive. "The most important measure is lowering the tax on dividends. In Israel you don't see investors who buy shares for 10 years just to get semiannual dividends."
He also predicted the tax on savings plans will not pass and said it would be difficult for institutional investors to invest abroad as they are suffering from low liquidity.
"The direction is right but implementation will be difficult," he said.
The Bank of Israel reiterated its position concerning the importance of stimulating savings, especially in a period when savings in Israel have been declining.
"Therefore it is not currently desirable to impose a new tax on savings of different durations," the central bank said in a statement.

"The Brodett committee's recommendations are positive and provide an important solution for some of the problems in the capital markets. It is unfortunate the recommendations address only the long term and provide no solution to what must happen tomorrow morning," said Danny Gillerman, president of the Federation of Israel Chambers of Commerce.
